title: Repaint a Connected Patch
statement:
An image is a grid of integers, image[r][c] being the colour of one pixel. You click the pixel at row sr, column sc with the paint-bucket tool and colour color.

The bucket repaints the clicked pixel and every pixel reachable from it by steps up, down, left or right through pixels of the clicked pixel's original colour. Diagonal neighbours are not connected. Return the image after the fill.

examples.why: The 3 in the bottom-left corner touches the patch only diagonally, so it keeps its colour.
The new colour equals the old one, so nothing changes. A fill that does not notice this can loop forever.
The clicked pixel has no neighbour of its colour, so only it changes.

hints: This is a graph search: pixels are nodes, and two pixels are connected when they are side by side and share the original colour.
Remember the original colour of the clicked pixel before you change anything. If it already equals the new colour, return right away.
Use a stack or a queue. Repaint a pixel when you push it, and only push neighbours inside the grid that still have the original colour. The repaint itself marks a pixel as visited.

explain.intuition:
The paint bucket in any drawing app is a graph search. Each pixel is a node, and it links to its four side neighbours when they have the same colour as the starting pixel. Everything reachable from the click gets the new colour.

You do not need a separate visited set: once a pixel is repainted it no longer has the original colour, so it is never pushed again. That trick fails in exactly one case, when the new colour equals the original one. Then nothing looks visited and the search runs forever, so return early. Use an explicit stack or queue rather than recursion: a 300 × 300 snake-shaped patch is 90 000 pixels deep, far more than a JavaScript call stack allows.
steps: Read orig = image[sr][sc]. If orig === color, return the image unchanged.
Paint the start pixel and push it on a stack.
Pop a pixel. For each of its four neighbours inside the grid with colour orig, paint it and push it.
When the stack is empty, return the image.
pitfalls: Not handling orig === color. Repainted pixels still match the original colour, so they are pushed again and again.
Counting diagonal neighbours. The first example's bottom-left 3 must stay.
Recursing once per pixel. On a large, winding patch this overflows the call stack.

complexity.space: O(rows · cols) for the stack in the worst case

solutions.title: Depth-first with an explicit stack
solutions.idea: Paint pixels as they are pushed; the new colour doubles as the visited mark.

solutions.title: Breadth-first with a queue
solutions.idea: The same search, spreading out ring by ring from the click like the fill animation in a paint app.

followups: Return the number of separate same-colour patches in the image. How does a fill help count them?
Only repaint the border of the patch, the pixels that touch a different colour or the edge. What extra check do you need?
